title: The State of Qatar
subtitle: 1971–today · Gas, Al Jazeera, the Blockade, the World Cup and the Mediator's Chair

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Three emirs of the Āl Thānī — a cautious founder deposed by his son, the son who remade the country with gas and Al Jazeera, and the grandson who held it through a blockade and delivered a World Cup — with the family's own men as prime ministers

entries.label: Sheikh Khalīfa ibn Ḥamad
entries.hint: Took power from his cousin Aḥmad in a bloodless coup in 1972, ruled cautiously through the first oil decades, and began the natural-gas development that would transform the country — then was himself deposed by his son while abroad.
entries.note: the 1972 succession; Allen Fromherz, 'Qatar: A Modern History' (2012).

entries.label: Sheikh Hamad ibn Khalīfa
entries.hint: Deposed his father in a 1995 palace coup and remade Qatar — the LNG mega-expansion, Al Jazeera in 1996, the 2003 constitution, Education City, the museums, the 2010 World Cup bid, and a foreign policy far out of proportion to the country's size.
entries.note: Fromherz (2012); Mehran Kamrava, 'Qatar: Small State, Big Politics' (2013).

entries.label: Sheikh Tamīm ibn Ḥamad
entries.hint: Took over in June 2013 in a rare voluntary abdication, held the country together through the 2017–2021 blockade, delivered the 2022 World Cup, and made Qatar the indispensable mediator of the Gaza war. As of early 2026 he remains emir.
entries.note: the June 2013 abdication; this entry records the position as of early 2026.

entries.label: The Āl Thānī prime ministers
entries.hint: Sheikh Ḥamad ibn Jāsim — 'HBJ' — foreign minister and then prime minister, the architect of the activist foreign policy and the sovereign fund's early deals, until his removal in 2013; then Sheikh ʿAbdullāh ibn Nāṣir.
entries.note: the profiles of HBJ; the 2013 government change accompanying the abdication.

entries.label: Sheikh Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, prime minister
entries.hint: The long-serving foreign minister who added the premiership in 2023, and the public face of Qatar's mediation of Afghanistan, Ukraine and Gaza.
entries.note: the March 2023 appointment; the reporting on Qatar's Gaza mediation 2023–2025.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Successions decided inside the family, three failed attempts by the neighbours to bring Qatar to heel, the World Cup labour reckoning, and an Israeli strike on Doha

entries.label: The coups of 1972 and 1995
entries.hint: Khalīfa's bloodless removal of his cousin Aḥmad in 1972, and Hamad's bloodless removal of his father Khalīfa in 1995 while the emir was in Switzerland — Qatari successions decided inside the ruling family, by pre-emption.
entries.note: Fromherz (2012); the 1995 coup and the 2004 reconciliation with the exiled Khalīfa.

entries.label: The 1996 counter-coup attempt
entries.hint: A plot to restore Khalīfa, allegedly backed by Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Egypt, was foiled by the new emir — the first sign that Qatar's neighbours would not tolerate its independent course under Hamad.
entries.note: the 1996 trials; Kamrava, 'Qatar: Small State, Big Politics' (2013).

entries.label: The 2017–2021 blockade
entries.hint: Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Egypt cut all land, sea and air links and issued thirteen demands — close Al Jazeera, downgrade Iran ties, expel Turkish troops, end support for Islamists — which Qatar refused. The siege lasted three and a half years.
entries.note: the thirteen demands (June 2017); the Al-Ula declaration ending the crisis (5 January 2021).

entries.label: The World Cup labour reckoning
entries.hint: The decade of construction for 2022 drew sustained international scrutiny of migrant deaths and the kafala system — a few dozen 'work-related' deaths by the official count against advocacy estimates in the thousands from all causes — and forced the most significant labour reforms in the Gulf.
entries.note: the Guardian and Amnesty International investigations; the ILO reporting on Qatar; the disputed death-toll figures (flagged: counts differ by definition).

entries.label: The 2025 Israeli strike on Doha
entries.hint: An Israeli airstrike on Hamas's negotiating team in the Qatari capital — an attack on the territory of a US ally hosting the ceasefire talks, and a sharp widening of the Gaza war's regional reach.
entries.note: the September 2025 strike and the international reaction; contemporary reporting.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The constitution and the Shura Council that was elected once and then unelected, the gas institutions, the sovereign fund, and the labour reforms

entries.label: The 2003 Constitution and the Shura Council
entries.hint: A permanent constitution approved by referendum, promising a partly elected consultative assembly — which was not elected until 2021, when the tribal-eligibility rules sparked rare protests, and which a 2024 referendum then reverted to fully appointed.
entries.note: the 2003 constitution; the October 2021 Shura elections and the 2024 amendment.

entries.label: The North Field and QatarEnergy
entries.hint: The 1971 discovery of the North Field, the 1977 moratorium and its lifting, the phased LNG build-out with the international majors, and the state company that runs it — the institutional machinery behind the wealth, and the North Field expansion now under way.
entries.note: the QatarEnergy (formerly Qatar Petroleum) history; the North Field East and South expansion projects.

entries.label: The Qatar Investment Authority
entries.hint: The 2005 sovereign fund and its high-profile holdings — Harrods, the Shard, a Barclays stake, Volkswagen, Paris Saint-Germain, Sainsbury's — turning gas revenue into visible influence in the boardrooms of London, Paris and Berlin.
entries.note: the Qatar Investment Authority; the sovereign-wealth-fund league tables.

entries.label: The labour reforms of 2017–2020
entries.hint: A non-discriminatory minimum wage, the removal of the exit-permit and no-objection-certificate requirements, an ILO office in Doha, and worker-support funds — the most far-reaching kafala reforms in the Gulf, though enforcement has lagged the law.
entries.note: the ILO–Qatar technical cooperation programme; Law No. 17 of 2020 (minimum wage); the 2020 removal of the NOC requirement.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: A lighter-touch Wahhābism, the long shelter given to the Muslim Brotherhood, and the quiet toleration of the migrant majority's faiths

entries.label: State Islam, the permissive version
entries.hint: Qatar shares the Ḥanbalī–Wahhābī tradition with Saudi Arabia but applies it far more lightly — churches on a designated compound since 2008, alcohol in licensed venues, no religious police with arrest powers — a calculated distance from the Saudi model.
entries.note: Fromherz (2012) on Qatari Wahhābism; the 2008 opening of the Religious Complex in Doha.

entries.label: Qatar and the Muslim Brotherhood
entries.hint: Doha hosted Yūsuf al-Qaraḍāwī, the Brotherhood's most influential cleric, for decades, funded Islamist movements across the Arab Spring, and gave the Brotherhood a platform on Al Jazeera — the single biggest source of its rupture with the UAE, Egypt and Saudi Arabia.
entries.note: David Roberts, 'Qatar and the Muslim Brotherhood's Global Affiliation Network'; al-Qaraḍāwī died in Doha in 2022.

entries.label: Faith in a country nine-tenths foreign
entries.hint: The churches on the Religious Complex, and the temples and gurdwaras of the South Asian majority worshipping more quietly — the religious life of the roughly 88 percent of residents who are not citizens.
entries.note: the US State Department International Religious Freedom reports on Qatar.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Museums and universities bought at scale, an instant city for display, the curated pearling past, and a small arts scene with a hard boundary

entries.label: The museums and Education City
entries.hint: The Museum of Islamic Art by I. M. Pei (2008), the National Museum of Qatar by Jean Nouvel (2019), Mathaf, and the branch campuses of Georgetown, Cornell-Weill, Northwestern and Texas A&M in Education City — culture and knowledge acquired at scale as soft power.
entries.note: the Qatar Foundation and Education City; the Qatar Museums projects.

entries.label: The Doha skyline and Msheireb
entries.hint: The West Bay towers, the rebuilt downtown of Msheireb, Katara cultural village, and the eight World Cup stadiums — an instant city built as a stage, on a peninsula that was mostly bare a lifetime ago.
entries.note: the Msheireb Downtown Doha regeneration; the 2022 World Cup stadium programme.

entries.label: Al Zubarah and the pearling past
entries.hint: The excavated 18th- and 19th-century pearling and trading town on the northwest coast, a UNESCO site, and the falconry, the sadu weaving and the desert heritage a new state curates against its own newness.
entries.note: the UNESCO inscription of 'Al Zubarah Archaeological Site' (2013); the Qatar–Denmark excavations.

entries.label: The Qatari arts scene and its limit
entries.hint: The Doha Film Institute and the Ajyal festival, the visual arts around Mathaf, and the poetry — including the case of Muḥammad al-ʿAjamī, jailed in 2012 for a poem read as an insult to the emir and pardoned in 2016, which marked the boundary of the opening.
entries.note: the Doha Film Institute; the case of the poet Muḥammad al-ʿAjamī (Ibn al-Dhīb).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The channel that broke the Arab state monopoly on news, the small-state strategy as a case study, and the most scrutinised labour system in the Gulf

entries.label: Al Jazeera and the Arab public sphere
entries.hint: The 1996 launch of the first pan-Arab satellite channel not censored on behalf of other Arab regimes — it broke the state monopoly on Arab news, amplified the Arab Spring, and became a diplomatic weapon the 2017 blockading states demanded be silenced.
entries.note: Marc Lynch, 'Voices of the New Arab Public' (2006); Hugh Miles, 'Al-Jazeera' (2005).

entries.label: The small-state strategy
entries.hint: Qatar as the textbook case of a micro-state using wealth, a global media outlet, a foreign military base, strategic hedging and relentless soft-power investment to acquire influence and security disproportionate to its size.
entries.note: Kamrava, 'Qatar: Small State, Big Politics' (2013); the small-state international-relations literature.

entries.label: The labour-rights record
entries.hint: The Guardian, Amnesty International and ILO investigations of the World Cup construction, the dispute over the death toll, and the assessment of the 2020 reforms — the most scrutinised labour system anywhere in the Gulf.
entries.note: the ILO 'One is too many' reporting on Qatari workplace deaths; the human-rights-organisation assessments (advocacy sources, flagged).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: One gas field that made a country the richest per capita on earth, the gas-to-liquids bet, the sovereign fund abroad, the blockade's self-sufficiency drive, and the World Cup and Ukraine windfalls

entries.label: The North Field and the LNG superpower
entries.loc: the North Field · and Ras Laffan
entries.hint: The world's largest non-associated gas field, shared with Iran, made Qatar the world's largest LNG exporter from 2006 and, per capita, one of the richest countries on earth — an economy resting almost entirely on one field.
entries.note: the Qatargas and RasGas histories; the LNG export data.

entries.label: Gas-to-liquids
entries.hint: The Pearl GTL plant with Shell, the world's largest, and Oryx GTL — Qatar's wager that converting gas to synthetic diesel and base oils would diversify the product mix beyond LNG.
entries.note: the Pearl GTL project (Shell / QatarEnergy); Oryx GTL.

entries.label: The sovereign fund abroad
entries.hint: An estimated half a trillion dollars in assets, from London property to European carmakers to a Paris football club — the visible instrument of Qatari influence in the world's capitals, and a hedge against the end of gas.
entries.note: the QIA disclosures and estimates; the high-profile European acquisitions.

entries.label: The blockade economy
entries.hint: The 2017 siege forced Qatar to reroute trade through Oman and Turkey, fly in dairy herds, and invest in domestic food production — Baladna, vertical farms, greenhouses — a crash course in economic autonomy that outlasted the reconciliation.
entries.note: the reporting on Qatar's blockade-era supply chains; the Baladna dairy project.

entries.label: The World Cup and the Ukraine windfall
entries.hint: An estimated 200-plus billion dollars spent on infrastructure for the 2022 tournament, and the LNG price surge after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine that made Qatar the courted supplier of a Europe cut off from Russian gas.
entries.note: the 2022 World Cup infrastructure-cost estimates; the 2022–23 LNG price and the European supply agreements.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Outdoor cooling in a country that would otherwise be uninhabitable, an airline that made a peninsula a global hub, and the highest carbon footprint on earth

entries.label: Cooling the outdoors
entries.hint: The air-conditioned World Cup stadiums, the shaded and misted public spaces and bus stops, and the near-total dependence on cooling in a country that would otherwise be barely habitable through the summer.
entries.note: the 2022 stadium cooling systems; the studies of outdoor air-conditioning in the Gulf.

entries.label: Qatar Airways and the aviation hub
entries.hint: The state airline built from 1997 into one of the world's largest long-haul carriers, and Hamad International Airport — the connectivity that makes a small peninsula a global transit point and a soft-power platform.
entries.note: the Qatar Airways fleet and route data; Hamad International Airport (opened 2014).

entries.label: The highest carbon footprint on earth
entries.hint: Gas flaring, desalination, air-conditioning and a huge hydrocarbon output divided among a small population give Qatar the world's highest per-capita CO2 emissions — a structural fact its climate diplomacy has to work around.
entries.note: the Global Carbon Project per-capita emissions data; the North Field emissions debate.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The US base that has twice deterred the neighbours, three failed attempts to bring Qatar to heel, the working relationships with Iran and Turkey, and the mediation of everyone's wars

entries.label: Qatar and the United States
entries.loc: Al Udeid Air Base, Qatar · and Washington
entries.hint: Al Udeid Air Base, built from 2003 as the forward headquarters of US Central Command, and major-non-NATO-ally status granted in 2022 — the security guarantee that has twice deterred Qatar's neighbours from going further than a blockade.
entries.note: Al Udeid Air Base; the January 2022 major-non-NATO-ally designation.

entries.label: Qatar and the Gulf rivalry
entries.hint: The 1996 counter-coup attempt, the 2014 withdrawal of ambassadors, and the 2017–21 blockade — three attempts by Saudi Arabia and the UAE to force Qatar back into line, all of which failed, ending with the Al-Ula reconciliation of 2021.
entries.note: the 2014 GCC ambassadorial crisis; the 2017–21 blockade and the Al-Ula declaration.

entries.label: Qatar and Iran
entries.hint: The shared North Field, an air and sea corridor that kept Qatar supplied through the blockade, and a working relationship that the blockading states cited as a grievance and that Qatar has never abandoned.
entries.note: the North Field / South Pars shared reservoir; the 2017 Iranian air corridor.

entries.label: Qatar and Turkey
entries.hint: The Turkish military base opened in 2015, the troops and food flown in during the blockade, and a strategic partnership between the two governments most aligned with the region's Islamist movements.
entries.note: the Qatar–Turkey Combined Joint Force Command base (2015); the 2017 emergency deployment.

entries.label: The mediator of last resort
entries.hint: The Taliban office in Doha and the 2020 US–Taliban agreement, the 2021 Kabul evacuation, the Chad, Sudan, DRC, Iran–US and Venezuela talks, and — since 2023 — the central role in the Gaza hostage and ceasefire negotiations, hosting Hamas's political office throughout.
entries.note: the February 2020 Doha Agreement (US–Taliban); the reporting on Qatar's Gaza mediation 2023–2025.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The fullest realisation of the small-state playbook, the blockade that showed the limits of Gulf unity, and reforms that stalled while the diplomacy grew

entries.label: The small state that punched above its weight
entries.hint: Qatar turned a tiny population and a single gas field into a global media network, a sovereign fund in the world's boardrooms, a US base, a World Cup and the indispensable diplomatic broker of two wars — the fullest realisation of the micro-state playbook.
entries.note: Kamrava, 'Qatar: Small State, Big Politics' (2013).

entries.label: The blockade and the limits of Gulf unity
entries.hint: The 2017 siege by fellow GCC states showed that the Gulf monarchies' shared interests stop where their rivalries begin — and that a small state with the right patrons and the right assets can defy its larger neighbours and win.
entries.note: the analyses of the 2017 crisis and its resolution; Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, 'Qatar and the Gulf Crisis' (2020).

entries.label: The reforms that stalled and the diplomacy that grew
entries.hint: As of the mid-2020s Qatar has rolled its Shura Council back to fully appointed and let the labour reforms' enforcement slip, while its mediation role — Afghanistan, Ukraine, Gaza — has become more central to the region than ever.
entries.note: the 2024 constitutional amendment; the continuing ILO and rights-group assessments of the labour reforms. This entry records the situation as of early 2026 and makes no prediction.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The migrant workforce and the reforms, the argument over the World Cup dead, citizens as a tenth of the country, and the boundary of the opening for women and poets

entries.label: The migrant workforce and the kafala reforms
entries.hint: Non-citizens are roughly 88 percent of Qatar's population and almost the entire private-sector workforce. The 2017–2020 reforms — minimum wage, no exit permit, no NOC — were real on paper, and the gap between the law and the workplace is the subject of continuing dispute.
entries.note: the ILO–Qatar programme reports; the Migrant-Rights.org and Human Rights Watch reporting (advocacy sources, flagged).

entries.label: The World Cup dead
entries.hint: The argument over how many workers died building the tournament — the official count of work-related deaths against the total number of migrant deaths from all causes over the decade — became a proxy for the ethics of the whole project.
entries.note: the Guardian's 2021 investigation; the Qatari government's and the tournament organisers' responses; the definitional dispute over what counts.

entries.label: Citizens as a tenth of the country
entries.hint: Qatari nationals are around 300,000 of nearly three million residents — a hyper-privileged minority with citizenship, welfare and a share in the gas — and the question of what a national identity means at that ratio runs through Qatari public life.
entries.note: the Qatar Planning and Statistics Authority population data; the identity debates in the Qatari press.

entries.label: Women, the poet and the limits of the opening
entries.hint: Qatari women's very high university enrolment and public visibility, alongside the male-guardianship rules a 2021 Human Rights Watch report and a 2024 domestic campaign challenged — and, on the other side, the jailing of the poet al-ʿAjamī: the boundary of the 'opening'.
entries.note: Human Rights Watch, 'Everything I Have to Do is Tied to a Man' (2021) (advocacy source, flagged); the al-ʿAjamī case.
